Selling a house in Jackson

Mississippi's capital and most populous city, Jackson, lies on the Pearl River in the center of the state. Most of it lies in northeastern Hinds County, where it shares the county seat role with Raymond. Slivers extend into Rankin County, home to the airport, and Madison County, home to Tougaloo College.

At about 113 square miles, Jackson is big and uneven. Ridgeland is north, Flowood and Richland are east, Byram is south and Clinton is west. Interstates 55 and 20 meet near downtown, with Interstate 220 and U.S. 49, 51 and 80 filling out the grid. Downtown's Union Station serves Amtrak's City of New Orleans along with Greyhound and the city's buses.

Public schools are mostly run by Jackson Public Schools, but some Hinds County addresses fall into other districts. If a buyer asks which district serves your address, check rather than guess.

The 2020 census recorded 153,701 residents, down 11.42 percent from 173,514 in 2010. In a city that has shrunk, the street you live on counts for a lot, and two houses a mile apart can sell on very different terms.

Jackson's water system and your sale

A federal court supervises the city's water system. More than 71,000 connections depend on it, and repairs are still under way at both treatment plants and across the distribution network. When the system failed in 2022, tens of thousands of people went without running water for weeks.

On November 29, 2022 the court entered an Interim Stipulated Order agreed to by the EPA, the Department of Justice, the Mississippi State Department of Health and the City. It put an Interim Third-Party Manager in charge of operations, working through JXN Water, with a list of priority projects. Fixes to distribution leaks have cut average daily demand by 25 percent, and corrosion control treatment is finished at the J.H. Fewell plant.

Expect buyers to ask about pressure, boil water notices and plumbing. Hold on to recent water bills, jot down any past notices you remember, and answer plainly. JXN Water posts billing, customer service and boil water information, and the Health Department posts compliance reports. A cash buyer who takes the house as is does not need your plumbing to satisfy a lender.

Hail, wind and drainage

Storms, rain and soil are what buyers' inspectors tend to chase in Jackson. Much of the city sits on acidic silt loam, and the Pearl River runs along the east side with the Ross Barnett Reservoir to the northeast.

  • A roof's hail and wind claim history is part of the house's record, so keep the claim paperwork.
  • Foundation movement and poor drainage are frequent reasons buyers ask for credits in silty soil.
  • Look up the flood designation before you guess at insurance costs, especially near the river or a creek.

Code enforcement and rental registration

The Office of Code Services applies the 2018 International Property Maintenance Code with local changes. Its Community Improvement division aims for voluntary compliance, goes to court as a last resort, and spends federal, state and local money to repair violations on properties held by absentee owners. Eight enforcement beats cover the city, each with its own officer.

The city council passes resolutions declaring particular parcels a menace to public health, safety and welfare under Section 21-19-11 of the Mississippi Code, then authorizes cleanup or demolition. Call the code office and ask whether costs for either have been assessed against your parcel.

Landlords have another duty. Jackson relaunched rental registration, which calls for a local agent who can act for the owner and produces a Rental Certificate. Rentals now outnumber owner-occupied homes in the city. Make sure a rental house is registered before you sell, and tell any buyer if it is not.

Hinds County tax due dates and penalties

The county mails statements during the first week of December. Full payment is due on or before February 1, and each month after that adds a half percent penalty, even on installments. The postmark decides whether you were late. If no bill arrives, call the county tax collector at (601) 968-6591.

The statement carries the name of whoever owned the property on January 1, which is why a buyer may see a previous owner's name on a receipt. Title companies normally divide the year's tax between buyer and seller at closing.

Selling with taxes owed

Delinquent parcels can be sold at the tax sale, and Hinds County publishes both a delinquent list and a tax sale list. State law permits sales on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August. Call the tax collector for the current schedule, and ask for a payoff figure early so the balance can come out of your sale proceeds.

Ways to sell a Jackson house quickly

You can list the house, sell it yourself or take a cash offer. Which one works often depends on the property's condition and paperwork. Sections 89-1-501 through 89-1-523 of the Mississippi Code call for a covered seller to hand over a written property condition disclosure statement before title passes. Be accurate, because buyers may ask about water service and storm history.

Cash sales are common for inherited houses, vacant houses, houses with open code cases and rentals with registration problems. A cash buyer can take the house as is and deal with city notices afterward, but you still pay liens from the proceeds and tell the buyer about violations you know of.

If the house has a water or plumbing history, tell the buyer up front. A repair the buyer learns about from you is a negotiating point. A repair the buyer finds on a closing-week inspection can stall the deal or end it.

Compare offers by what you keep, not by the number on the front page. Get terms in writing, ask who covers closing costs, and take your time. We make no price promises, and you can turn any offer down.

What to have ready for a closing

A Jackson sale usually runs in four steps: contract, title search, payoff, signing. Nothing about that order changes with a cash buyer, though the lender's appraisal and approval stage drops out. The title search lists liens, unpaid taxes and any city assessments, so you learn early what has to be paid from the proceeds. Bring identification, your mortgage payoff details if you have a loan, recent water bills, and records of past repairs or insurance claims. If a rental is involved, bring proof of registration and the Rental Certificate.

Frequently asked questions

Which counties is Jackson in?

Most of Jackson is in Hinds County, where it shares the county seat with Raymond. Small portions reach into Rankin County and Madison County.

When are Hinds County property taxes due?

Payment is due on or before February 1. After that date a half percent penalty applies each month, and a postmark after February 1 counts as late.

Does the water situation affect selling a Jackson house?

Buyers may ask about it. A court-ordered manager runs the system, repairs continue, and JXN Water posts boil water notices. Keep your bills and answer questions honestly.

Do I have to register a rental house in Jackson before selling it?

The city requires rental registration and issues a Rental Certificate. Check your status with the Office of Code Services and tell a buyer about any problem.

Can I sell a Jackson house with code violations?

Yes. Open violations and any city cleanup liens are usually settled from the proceeds at closing, so ask the code office what is outstanding. An as-is cash sale is a common way to handle it.

Gulfport and its neighborhoods

Gulfport is a port city on the Mississippi Sound in Harrison County, and it is one of the county's two seats. The 2020 count was 72,926 residents. The city covers 64.2 square miles, of which 56.9 are land, with Interstate 10 across the middle, U.S. 90 along the coast and U.S. 49 ending in town from the north.

Annexation drew the map. Gulfport took in the older settlements of Mississippi City and Handsboro in 1965, and in December 1993 it added 33 square miles to the north, including the historic community of Turkey Creek. A house can therefore sit near the beach, along a bayou or in a newer northern subdivision, and each setting brings its own insurance, flood and repair questions. Which school district a house falls into, Gulfport or Harrison County, depends on the address, so confirm it before you tell a buyer.

For land records, Harrison County has two judicial districts. The Chancery Clerk's first district office for recording and redemption is at 1801 23rd Avenue in Gulfport.

Hurricane history and the age of the houses

Two hurricanes reset the building stock. Camille in August 1969 pushed 21 feet of storm water into the waterfront areas and nearly destroyed the port. Katrina in August 2005 brought winds of at least 100 miles per hour and a surge of at least 19 feet, and 9,571 houses in the city were damaged or destroyed.

Many homes standing today were rebuilt or repaired after 2005. If you own one, find out what work was permitted, who did it and whether the paperwork is in a drawer. Buyers and their lenders will ask the same things.

Gulf weather and repair items

Humid heat and frequent rain wear on a Gulfport house, and tropical storms are the main severe weather risk. Four things get the most attention:

  • Roof coverings, flashing and vents after wind events.
  • Air conditioning systems that run most of the year.
  • Wood trim, siding and crawl spaces where moisture collects.
  • Windows and doors that must seal against driven rain.

An owner who has put this work off may find a traditional sale stalls at inspection. That is one reason some Gulfport sellers look at an as-is cash sale instead.

Code enforcement and neglected property

The city checks properties against state law, city ordinances and zoning rules, and it says it prefers voluntary compliance. Complaints arrive through the 311 system, by phone at (228) 868-5718, or from staff who spot problems on their rounds. An officer typically visits within 24 hours to see whether a violation exists.

Gulfport applies the International Property Maintenance Code with a local amendment adopted as Ordinance 2812. Inspectors look at the outside of the property. They need your signed consent to enter, or a court warrant if access is denied and necessary.

After a notice, the city's FAQ describes your options:

  • Ask the inspector named on your compliance letter for more time. Extensions are routinely granted for hiring a contractor or special circumstances.
  • Meet the inspector on site to go over the violation, and contest charges at a council hearing before the hearing or court date.
  • If violations stay unresolved, the city can issue a citation or correct the problem itself through the City Council process, which may lead to fines or a lien on the property.

A lien from city cleanup has to be dealt with at or before closing. Read any notice you have received and keep your response in writing.

Property taxes in Gulfport

Harrison County bills real property taxes on December 1, and they are due by February 1 without interest. Interest of one half percent per month starts February 2. The county accepts payments until the Friday before its tax sale on the last Monday of August.

The bill is true value times assessment ratio times millage rate. Class I covers a single-family home lived in by its owner and uses 10 percent of true value, while Class II covers everything else at 15 percent. Every parcel must be revalued by the assessor at least once in four years.

Ask your agent or attorney whether your sale falls under those sections.

The deed is recorded with the Harrison County Chancery Clerk, and a title search usually comes before closing. Outstanding liens, unpaid taxes and heirs who never signed off are the most common reasons a Gulfport closing slips.

A practical order of work: pull your deed and any mortgage statement, get the tax balance from the Harrison County Tax Collector, ask the city whether any code notice is open on the address, and gather permit and repair records, especially anything done after 2005. With those four items in hand, any buyer, agent or investor can give you a clear answer faster.

Is Gulfport the county seat of Harrison County?

Yes, Gulfport is one of two county seats. Harrison County moved its seat to Gulfport in 1902, and the Chancery Clerk keeps land records in both Gulfport and Biloxi.

By February 1 each year without interest. Bills go out from Harrison County on December 1, and interest at 0.5 percent a month starts on February 2.

Yes. Open violations and city cleanup liens generally get resolved, disclosed or paid from your proceeds at closing, so find out from the code office what is still open. Inspectors will generally discuss an extension if you contact the officer on your notice.

What happens if I miss the Harrison County tax sale deadline?

The property is listed for the tax sale on the last Monday of August and offered to registered tax purchasers. You stay the legal owner during the two-year redemption period, but you must pay the taxes, interest and fees to redeem.

Selling a house in Southaven

On the Mississippi side of the state line, Southaven is a DeSoto County city roughly 14 miles south of downtown Memphis. As a principal city of Greater Memphis, it has many owners who work, shop and fly out of Tennessee yet pay their taxes in Mississippi. Residents numbered 54,648 in 2020 and an estimated 57,493 in 2024, which ranks Southaven third in Mississippi and first among Memphis suburbs.

The city covers about 41.5 square miles. Interstate 55, which also carries the I-69 designation, runs north to south through it, with U.S. 51 and Mississippi Highway 302 as other main roads. The airport at Memphis International lies about two miles north of the city's center point, with approach paths from both north-south runways running right over town. Noise questions from buyers are common.

Incorporation came in 1980, after Memphis homebuilder Kemmons Wilson laid out subdivisions of small starter homes just across the state line. In the years that followed, the city doubled its land area while its population tripled. Southaven Towne Center opened in October 2007 and Tanger Outlets Southaven in November 2015. Because homes went up over several decades, repair needs differ from street to street, and a seller usually hears about them from the buyer's inspection report. A house that struggles through inspection is where an as-is cash sale often comes up.

What buyers' inspectors check first

Long hot summers, frequent rain and past storm damage push roofs and drainage to the top of most inspection reports, so walk the property with those in mind. Nearly 55 inches of rain fall in a year, with April the wettest month, and an EF-2 tornado touched down in Southaven on February 5, 2008.

  • Roofs: look for lifted shingles and granule loss after storm seasons.
  • Drainage: standing water near the slab or crawl space often shows up in inspections.
  • HVAC: long cooling seasons put heavy wear on air conditioners.

Living between two states

Plenty of Southaven households have a Tennessee job, doctor or school connection. When you sell, remember that the house, the tax bill and the deed are all in Mississippi, so Mississippi rules apply even if your agent, lawyer or lender is across the line. Confirm that whoever handles your closing is comfortable with DeSoto County recording and tax practices. The state formula counts 10 percent of true value for a house its owner lives in and 15 percent for any other real property, a rental included. County, city and school district each set a millage rate, and all three apply to the assessed value. A bigger bill can come from a higher value, a higher rate, or both.

  • The DeSoto County Tax Collector's number is 662-469-8030.
  • Tax sale day is the last Monday in August, with bidding handled on an online platform run with GovEase.

A parcel sold at tax sale has a clouded title, and that generally must be cleared before you can close. Ask the DeSoto office how redemption works on your parcel before you rely on it.

If you dispute an assessment, the Chancery Clerk can explain how to get a Board of Supervisors hearing, which is normally requested by the first Monday in August.

Homestead exemption after a sale

Your exemption stays with you. The next owner has to file with the county Tax Assessor from January 1 to April 1, because it is never automatic. The filer needs to own the house and live there as a primary residence on January 1, and the deed has to be on file at the Chancery Clerk before January 7. When an inspector turns up problems, you cut the price, pay for repairs or lose the buyer. A direct as-is sale removes that fork in the road. Ask any buyer to put the offer in writing, and keep the paperwork you have been given.

Costs of waiting

An empty Southaven house still produces bills. Property tax, insurance, utilities and lawn care continue each month whether or not a buyer shows up, and a long listing period adds up. Stack those carrying costs against the gap between listing and cash prices, and ask what a few extra months would truly cost.

Disclosure and selling as is

Mississippi Code section 89-1-503 obliges the seller to deliver the written property condition disclosure statement ahead of the title transfer. If the statement comes after an offer, the buyer can cancel within three days of hand delivery or five of mailing.

A cash sale as is leaves that duty in place and only changes who pays for repairs. Cash Home Buyers works with Southaven sellers who would rather sell the house in its present condition than manage contractors, and we explain the terms in writing before anyone commits.

Even so, the closing path is familiar: a title search surfaces liens and unpaid taxes, they are paid from your proceeds, you sign the deed, and the Chancery Clerk records it. No. Each new owner files separately during the January 1 to April 1 window, and has to own and live in the home on January 1 of the tax year.

A city split between two counties

Hattiesburg is the seat of Forrest County and the center of the Pine Belt in south Mississippi. Most of the city lies in Forrest County, and a smaller western portion, much of it commercial land added in a 2008 annexation, lies in Lamar County. The 2020 count was 48,730 residents.

Why it matters: your tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk all depend on which county holds your parcel. Confirm the county first, before you ask a title company to prorate taxes or record a deed.

Demand comes from several directions: the University of Southern Mississippi, William Carey University, health care, manufacturing and Camp Shelby south of the city. Student housing and rentals are part of the market, and some sellers are landlords ready to stop managing a rental. If that is you, check lease status and deposits before you sell. A written record of the lease terms helps a buyer and keeps the closing simple.

Older houses and historic districts

Hattiesburg grew around the railroads, and it has a historic core and a long list of older streets. The city has a Historic Conservation Commission and a design guidelines manual for historic districts, so a house in one of those districts may need a Certificate of Appropriateness before exterior work. Ask the city's planning office at 601-545-4599 whether your address is covered.

Before you list an older house, walk it with a critical eye and decide what you will fix, what you will disclose and what you will leave for the buyer. Fixes that need a permit should be permitted, and receipts should be kept. Older homes bring familiar repair items: original wiring, galvanized or cast iron plumbing and settled foundations. A buyer's lender may balk at these. An investor buying for cash usually does not.

Tornado history and your records

Spring thunderstorms here can bring heavy rain, large hail and tornadoes. An EF4 tornado on February 10, 2013 formed in Lamar County and moved east into Hattiesburg, causing EF1 to EF3 damage near the University of Southern Mississippi campus and in neighborhoods just north of downtown. An EF3 tornado struck early on January 21, 2017.

Seller-side effects of that history include these:

  • Insurance claim files, contractor invoices and permits should stay with the house paperwork.

A permit is generally required to build, repair or alter a residence, though some routine repairs may not need one. The Urban Development Department handles planning, zoning, permits, building inspections and code enforcement from City Hall at 200 Forrest Street. The building division number is 601-554-1003, and code enforcement is 601-554-1027.

Zoning follows the city's Land Development Code, and the building code is the 2018 International Residential Code. Permitted work must be inspected before it is covered, and the city asks for at least 24 hours of notice for an inspection.

One item deserves a seller's attention. The city's residential page says an owner who acts as his or her own contractor on a single-family home may be subject to the Mississippi Home Warranty Act and, if the home is later sold, may be required to warrant it for up to seven years from the sale date. If you built or added to your home yourself, talk with an attorney before you sell.

The city also publishes floodplain information. If your property is near the Leaf or Bouie rivers, ask about its flood designation.

Taxes in both counties are due by February 1. The Forrest County Tax Collector is at 601 N. Main Street in downtown Hattiesburg, and Lamar County gives February 1 as the last day to pay without interest.

Flood and permit rules before you repair

Building, altering, regrading or filling a Biloxi lot takes a permit from the city's Building Division, and homes in a flood hazard area face stricter standards. The city's flood bulletin says work under $500 carries no permit fee and that new buildings in the floodplain must sit one foot above the base flood elevation.

The rule that surprises sellers is the 50 percent test. When additions, remodeling or repairs to an existing structure add up to 50 percent or more of its market value, the whole building has to meet new-construction standards. A storm-damaged house in a mapped flood zone can cost far more to fix for resale than the visible damage suggests.

Before work starts, write down what is being repaired, what it costs and who is doing it, and keep the permits and receipts together. Standard homeowner's insurance does not pay for flood damage. The city's flood bulletin points owners to a separate National Flood Insurance Program policy. Brandon's page says state law requires a residential builder's license for a home above $50,000 and a residential or remodeler's license for a remodel above $10,000. An owner can pull a permit personally, but that makes the owner the general contractor, with personal liability for accidents on the job.

  • New residential permits are often issued within 24 hours of submittal.
  • A permit generally expires after 90 days if no inspections have been made.
  • A project counts as abandoned if no work is completed over a year.
  • Contractors register with the city, post a $5,000 performance bond and pay a $25 annual fee for each registered trade.

Inspectors work from the 2018 International Building, Residential, Property Maintenance, Mechanical, Plumbing, Fuel Gas and Fire codes, together with the 2017 National Electrical Code. Past work done without a permit can hold up a buyer who needs financing. Ask the department which permits are on file for your address before you list. The city permits page is the place to start.

Rental inspections and property upkeep

Brandon inspects single-family rental houses for fire safety and general maintenance under city ordinances. The forms list includes an Application for Rental Inspection and Permit, so a landlord who is selling should confirm the inspection record is current.

Code enforcement covers waste accumulation, unsanitary conditions, abandoned vehicles and noxious weeds on private property. A junk-filled or overgrown lot can bring a notice, and a vacant house that sits for months is the kind of property that draws one.

  • Walk the property and clear debris, dead vehicles and tall weeds.
  • Ask for any open complaint or violation notice in writing.
  • Collect past rental inspection results if the house was leased.
  • Keep receipts for permitted work.

One more rule applies near downtown: a sign in the historic district needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before the city will issue a sign permit.

Rankin County taxes for a Brandon seller

Real property taxes are paid to the Rankin County Tax Collector and are due February 1. When February 1 falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, paying the next Monday costs no penalty or interest.

The formula multiplies true value by the assessment ratio and by the millage rate. A house the owner lives in is assessed at 10 percent of true value; anything else is assessed at 15 percent. Because taxing entities set the millage where the property sits, equal-value houses in different parts of the county can carry different bills.

The county posts a notice for its delinquent tax land sale on the Tax Collector's news page. An owner who is behind should clear the balance before that sale, since unpaid real estate tax can send the property to auction. The Rankin County Tax Collector page lists office hours and payment methods.

Disclosure and deed recording

A seller of covered residential property delivers a written condition statement before title transfers. Timing comes from Section 89-1-503 of the Mississippi Code, and a note on the sales contract, the deposit receipt or an addendum shows the seller complied.

Deliver it after the offer and the buyer may cancel, within three days if it was handed over or five if it was mailed. Leave a section blank and the buyer is presumed to know to ask about it.

The Chancery Clerk records the deed. Since Rankin collects the $1.00 archive fee, the standard price for recording a deed is $26.00, and that covers indexing of the first five pages. Deeds must meet formatting rules, and an attorney-prepared instrument must carry the attorney's Mississippi Bar number.

In a typical sale the steps run in this order: gather the deed and tax receipt, sign the contract, let the title company search and clear any liens, then close and record. Anything owed on taxes or a mortgage is paid from your proceeds.

Is a cash sale a good fit in Brandon?

A cash sale is worth weighing when a listing would demand repairs, permits or time you do not have. Brandon's permit and inspection system rewards documented work. A well-kept house with a clean paper trail may do fine on the open market, while a house without one may be better as an as-is sale.

Listing the house brings showings, an agent, a buyer's inspection and a lender's appraisal, and any of those can add weeks or a repair request. A cash sale replaces most of that with one visit and one offer. The trade-off is price, because a cash buyer builds repair costs into the number, so compare the two paths on what you would actually net.

By February 1, paid to the Rankin County Tax Collector. If the date falls on a weekend or holiday, the cutoff becomes Monday, without penalty or interest.

Most likely, yes. The city lists re-roofing, siding, window replacements, decks and sheds as work that needs a building permit. Call Community Development at 601-824-4580 to confirm before you start.

Does Brandon inspect rental houses?

Yes. The city inspects single-family rentals for fire safety and maintenance under its ordinances, and landlords file an Application for Rental Inspection and Permit.

Selling a house in Starkville

Mississippi State University defines this market. Founded in 1878 as the state's land-grant college, the school turned Starkville from a farm town into a college town. Today the city, seat of Oktibbeha County in east-central Mississippi, leads the Golden Triangle region. The 2020 census found 24,360 residents in town and 51,427 in the whole county.

The median age was 28.7, and 40.8 percent of households were a single person. Buyers, renters and the school year all pull on a sale. In the county, owner-occupied homes have a median value of $171,500, and with 49 percent ownership about half of the housing is rented.

Timing a sale around the semester

Where the house sits decides who sees it. Near campus, the audience is students, parents, faculty and investors. Farther out, it is mostly families and university staff. Owner-held homes were vacant far less often than rentals in 2020, which tells you that the landlord with a house empty between leases is usually the one under the most time pressure.

  • A lease ending in May or August makes a clean handoff possible, or leaves a vacant house running up bills.
  • With tenants in place at closing, the buyer cares about the lease terms, so collect the lease and rent records early.
  • A house needing work between tenants often sells more smoothly to an as-is buyer than to a financed retail buyer.

Choose early between showing the house occupied or empty, and let that choice set your closing target.

Roads and older houses

U.S. 82 bypasses the city along its north side, running about 25 miles east to Columbus, and Mississippi Highways 12 and 25 also come through. Starkville has twenty-two National Register of Historic Places sites. An older house near downtown may carry a historic designation, which a buyer will want to hear about before planning exterior work, so ask city staff early.

The Cotton District and walkable neighborhoods

The Cotton District, begun in 1969 as a New Urbanist neighborhood near downtown, is a compact, walkable area with thousands of residential units and many restaurants and bars. Homes and units there sell on different logic from a suburban three-bedroom: investors study rent potential and student demand, while families look at yard size and school zoning. If you own there, expect questions about leases, parking and noise. If you own farther out, lean on space, quiet and commute.

Inherited or family-held houses

Heirs who share a Starkville house tend to get stuck on small questions: who may sign, whether taxes were paid, and where the deed was filed. Answer those first. Then gather repair receipts, tax bills and any lease, and decide together whether to list, sell to an investor or accept a cash offer. Write down what each heir expects before you talk to buyers, because a deal that is half agreed and then reopened costs weeks. An as-is buyer can close without anyone in the family spending money on repairs.

Property tax in Oktibbeha County

One county office values and collects. Payment is due February 1 for the prior assessment year. Both the Tax Assessor and the Collector work from 101 East Main Street in Starkville, and 662-323-1273 reaches them.

The Mississippi Constitution sets two ratios here. A single-family home its owner occupies falls in Class I and is taxed on 10 percent of true value. Other real property, including a house rented to students, is Class II at 15 percent. Combine the county, city and school district millage and apply it to the assessed value to reach the bill.

Landlords feel the difference most, since a rental pays on a larger share of value and a house that stops being owner-occupied can lose its homestead credit. Assessors revalue real property at least every four years. A disputed value goes to the Board of Supervisors, usually before the first Monday in August.

An unpaid bill can end in a tax sale. The state allows them on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, and the county Tax Collector can say which date applies to your parcel.

Homestead exemption and your closing

The exemption belongs to whoever lives in the house on January 1, so it does not pass to a buyer. Filing for a new owner happens at the Tax Assessor's office, January 1 to April 1. What counts is owning and living in the house as a primary residence on January 1, with the deed already on file at the Chancery Clerk before January 7.

Under-65 owners get a credit of up to $300. Anyone 65 or older, or totally disabled, owes nothing on the first $7,500 of assessed value, and some disabled service members and surviving spouses owe no tax on the home.

None of this helps an investor who buys a Starkville rental, because it will not be a primary residence. A family buying a first home early in the year may wait until the next year for the credit, a point worth raising during negotiation.

Disclosure and your sale options

Mississippi Code section 89-1-503 makes the seller hand the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement ahead of the title transfer. A buyer who gets it after making an offer can pull out in writing, within three days if it was handed over or five if it was mailed.

A Starkville owner has three main paths. Listing at retail can do well near campus, provided the house is in good order and the timing fits the academic year. A sale to another investor fits a rental with tenants. Going straight to a cash buyer as is means no repairs, no showings and no lender conditions.

A house that has stayed in a family for years deserves a close look at old deeds, unrecorded transfers and shared heirs while the title search is under way.

Questions to settle before accepting an offer

Before you say yes to anyone, answer five practical questions. Is the house vacant or leased, and until when? Are taxes current? Does the title search show anything besides your mortgage? Did any permit stay open? Who else has to sign? A seller with straight answers can compare offers calmly, whether they come from a retail buyer, an investor or a cash buyer, and can see quickly which one actually fits the calendar.

Title search, deed and closing

A title search comes first in any sale. Attorneys and title companies look for unpaid taxes, mortgages and liens and then draft the deed, which must carry a notarized seller signature and a legal description before the Chancery Clerk records it. Carry photo ID, tax receipts, a mortgage payoff figure if there is one, and copies of any leases.

Once you sign, whatever you owe is deducted from the proceeds and you keep the remainder. With a cash buyer there is no lender involved, so no step waits on a loan approval.

Can I sell a Starkville rental house with tenants in it?

Yes. The lease goes with the house, so hand the buyer the lease, deposit details and rent records. A few buyers want the place empty, so discuss timing first.

When are Oktibbeha County property taxes due?

The deadline is February 1 and covers the previous assessment year. A weekend or holiday deadline slides to the next Monday with no penalty.

Is a Starkville rental taxed differently from a home I live in?

Yes. Your own single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of true value; a rental and other real property are assessed at 15 percent.

Where do I pay property tax in Starkville?

Go to the combined Tax Assessor and Collector office on East Main Street, number 101, or phone 662-323-1273.

Typically so. The written property condition form is due before the title transfers, and a buyer who receives it late may cancel within three days of hand delivery or five days of mailing.
